scenes.name: El soul conquista Gran Bretaña
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 26 de octubre «Reach Out I’ll Be There» de los Four Tops, con la flauta de aire oriental, el fraseo dylaniano de Lamont Dozier y la interpretación de su vida de Levi Stubbs, desbancó a «Distant Drums» y fue número 1: el momento en que la música negra americana ocupó el centro de la cultura juvenil británica, al revés que en el boom del beat. Lo habían preparado durante años los entusiastas: Dave Godin, que fundó en 1963 la Tamla Motown Appreciation Society, viajó a Detroit, llevó «Where Did Our Love Go» a los piratas y bautizó el sello Tamla Motown (marzo de 1965, con una gira de la revista que fracasó fuera de Londres); Guy Stevens, que pinchaba discos negros en el Scene y dirigió Sue Records para Chris Blackwell; Roger Eagle en el Twisted Wheel de Mánchester; Tony Hall promocionando Atlantic («In the Midnight Hour», el «My Girl» de Otis Redding); el DJ Jeff Dexter mezclando soul y ska en Tiles, el club subterráneo de Oxford Street del mod de masas que visitó Tom Wolfe. En otoño de 1966 Atlantic y Motown copaban las listas; Otis Redding metió a 8.000 personas en Tiles; los Four Tops arrasaron en el Savile de Brian Epstein el 13 de noviembre. El racismo, aun así, seguía ahí.

podcast.title: Attempted Negotiation with Atlantic Records
podcast.body: At 16, after his group The Romeo's had a successful third single, "Fine Fine Fine," distributed by Atlantic, the label sought a follow-up. Dozier, believing he had negotiating power, demanded an album instead of just a single. Atlantic Records executive Jerry Wexler responded by releasing them from their contract, prematurely ending The Romeo's career. "But Lamont Dozier, at 16, thought that he had some kind of negotiating power, and wrote back saying they weren't interested in just doing a single, they wanted to do an album."

podcast.title: Cease and Desist for "Pop-I" Song
podcast.body: Dozier's first solo record under the name Lamont Anthony, released on Anna Records, was based on the comic character Popeye. As the song gained traction, King Features Syndicate, owners of Popeye, issued a cease and desist order. Dozier then re-recorded the vocal, changing the lyrics to "Benny the Skinny Man" instead of "Pop-I the Sailor Man," but the song subsequently flopped without the original hook. "Unfortunately, just as that record was starting to take off, King Feature's syndicate, The Owners of Pop-I, sent a cease and desist order, Dozier went back into the studio and recut the vocal, this time singing about Benny the Skinny Man instead of Pop-I the Sailor Man."

podcast.title: Early Musical Connections
podcast.body: Lamont Dozier grew up surrounded by musical people. In Hutchins Jr. High School, he was a couple of years younger than Motown's first star, Marv Johnson, knew Frieda Payne, and was classmates with Otis Williams (later of The Temptations). "At Hutchins, Jr. High School, he was a couple of years below Marv Johnson, the first Motown star."

podcast.title: Inspired by Aretha Franklin
podcast.body: As a junior high student, Dozier was profoundly inspired by his classmate, 14-year-old Aretha Franklin, after hearing her sing and play piano at church. This experience caused him to "radically revise his ideas of what it was possible for him to do" and pursue his own musical aspirations. "That 14-year-old Aretha Franklin, and as you can imagine, being classmates with someone who could perform like that caused the Motown Dozier to radically revise his ideas of what it was possible for him to do."

podcast.title: Musical Telepathy with Brian Holland
podcast.body: After joining Motown, Lamont Dozier and Brian Holland were introduced and quickly found an instant musical connection, discovering they had "musical telepathy." This led to their collaboration on "Forever" for The Marvelettes and formed the basis of their highly successful songwriting and production partnership. "The two instantly clicked musically. They discovered that they almost had a musical telepathy, and Holland got Freddie Garman, his lyricist partner at the time, to finish up the lyrics for the song, while he and Dozier came up with more ideas."

podcast.title: New Songwriting Partner for The Hollands
podcast.body: Lamont Dozier became a new writing partner for Brian and Eddie Holland, completing songs with them quickly and effectively ending Brian Holland's earlier songwriting partnership with Freddie Gorman. This trio would become the legendary Holland-Dozier-Holland team. "Freddie kept finding that when he came round to hit the film after work, if Brian Holland had had an idea for a song, he'd already finished it, usually with the help of his brother ready and their new writing partner, Lamont Dozier."

podcast.title: Odd Jobs at Anna Records
podcast.body: While singing with The Voice Masters, Lamont Dozier also worked for Anna Records, a Gordy family label, doing odd jobs such as cleaning floors. "And he'd continued to sing with them, as well as working for Anna Records doing odd jobs like cleaning the floors."

podcast.title: Skill for Riffs, Hooks, and Rhythms
podcast.body: Lamont Dozier possessed a great aptitude for creating both lyrical and musical riffs and hooks, as well as developing rhythmic ideas for songs. "Dozier had a great aptitude for coming up with riffs and hooks, both Liverpool and Musical, and rhythmic ideas, while Brian Holland could come up with great melodies and interesting chord changes, though both could do both."
